speaker: Priya
text: Okay, let's get started. This week's paper is Repurposing Geometric Foundation Models for Multi-view Diffusion. The method is called G L D, geometric latent diffusion.

speaker: Tom
text: Right. The pitch is that novel view synthesis models usually run diffusion in a VAE latent space, and that space has no idea about geometry. So each view is encoded on its own.

speaker: Kate
text: And their idea is to diffuse in the feature space of a geometric foundation model instead. They mainly use Depth Anything 3, and they try VGGT in the appendix.

speaker: Priya
text: Which I think is a neat move. Those features are already consistent across views, so the diffusion model doesn't have to learn the geometry from scratch.

speaker: Tom
text: The headline claim in figure one is that it converges about four point four times faster than training in the VAE space. I'm a little suspicious of convergence plots, but fine.

speaker: Kate
text: The thing I wanted to check is how much better the final numbers actually are. Do we remember the table?

speaker: Priya
text: Not off the top of my head. Atlas, what PSNR does G L D get on RealEstate ten K, compared to the VAE baseline?

speaker: Tom
text: While that comes up, the other piece is that the features have to be decoded back to pixels. They train a separate RGB decoder on top of the geometric features.

speaker: Kate
text: Yes, and they can decode depth as well, which is a nice side effect. You get geometry for free with every generated view.

speaker: Priya
text: So the model doesn't generate every level of the feature hierarchy. Depth Anything gives features at four levels, and they only synthesize up to a boundary level.

speaker: Tom
text: Right, and the rest of the network just runs on top of that. The question is where to put the boundary.

speaker: Kate
text: And they found that the deepest level, level three, works best as the synthesis boundary, because the deep features are the most abstract and the most geometric. That's the main ablation.

speaker: Tom
text: Makes sense to me. Abstract features should be easier for the diffusion model.

speaker: Priya
text: Okay. Let's talk about the evaluation setup, because I think that's where the skeptic in me wakes up.

speaker: Tom
text: They evaluate on RealEstate and DL3DV in domain, and Mip NeRF 360 out of domain. But RealEstate and DL3DV are also in the training data.

speaker: Kate
text: That's fair, although MVGenMaster also leans on an external depth estimator and isn't trained from scratch, so it cuts both ways.

speaker: Priya
text: Here's something I couldn't figure out. How many source views do they use in the main evaluation? Is it one view or several?

speaker: Tom
text: Hmm. I honestly don't remember. Kate, do you know?

speaker: Kate
text: No idea. It's probably buried in the setup section somewhere. Let's not get stuck on it.

speaker: Priya
text: Fine, let's move on. The other thing I wanted to discuss is the training compute.

speaker: Tom
text: They train on eight B two hundreds, for about a hundred and seventy five thousand iterations. Not cheap, but they do train from scratch on four datasets.

speaker: Kate
text: Hey Atlas, why did they need a separate cascaded model for level zero?

speaker: Priya
text: Good question, I was wondering about that too. It seems like extra machinery.

speaker: Tom
text: My guess is quality, but let's see what it says. Meanwhile, what did people think about the limitations section?

speaker: Kate
text: It's short. They admit it can hallucinate content in regions the source views never saw, for example with heavy occlusion, and that extreme lighting changes make correspondences unreliable.

speaker: Priya
text: I'd also like to know how it scales with more source views. The ablation goes from one to four views, and on RealEstate the gap to the VAE shrinks a bit.

speaker: Kate
text: Another open question for me is whether this works with a stronger video prior. Everything here is trained from scratch, so we don't know if it combines well with a large pretrained generator.

speaker: Tom
text: Agreed. And I'd want a runtime comparison. Sampling in a feature space with several levels might not be cheaper than a VAE at inference time, even if training converges faster.

speaker: Priya
text: They do have a computational cost section in the appendix, I think, but I only skimmed it. Let's each look at that before the next meeting.

speaker: Kate
text: One last thing I liked: the depth they decode is consistent with the generated images, so you can unproject the views into a point cloud and it actually looks coherent.

speaker: Tom
text: That's a good open question for the authors too, how far the geometry holds up with wider baselines. Should we wrap up there and pick next week's paper?

speaker: Priya
text: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
